claims.claim: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau defines a short sale as a type of loss mitigation in which the home is sold for less than what is owed on the mortgage, and describes it as an alternative to foreclosure in which the owner still has to leave the home.
claims.quotedLanguage: A short sale, which is a type of loss mitigation, is a sale of your home for less than what you owe on your mortgage. ... A short sale is an alternative to foreclosure, but because it is a sale, you will have to leave your home.
claims.notes: Consumer-education definition, not a statute. Attribute to the CFPB. The CFPB page carries its own disclaimer that it is general consumer information and not legal advice. Idaho Code sections read for this guide do not define 'short sale'.

claims.claim: The CFPB describes a short sale as depending on the lender's or servicer's agreement: if the lender or servicer agrees, the owner may be able to sell the home to pay off the mortgage even though the price or proceeds are less than the remaining balance.
claims.quotedLanguage: If your lender or servicer agrees to a short sale, you may be able to sell your home to pay off your mortgage, even if the sale price or proceeds turn out to be less than the balance remaining on your mortgage.
claims.notes: The condition is the lender's agreement. Never write that a seller or a buyer can 'do' a short sale without it, and never suggest this business can obtain that agreement. No approval timeline is sourced; do not state one.

claims.claim: The CFPB advises that in a state where the borrower is responsible for a deficiency, the borrower will want to ask the lender to waive the deficiency before going through with a short sale, that in some states the lender could sue after a short sale to collect it, and that any waiver should be obtained in writing and kept.
claims.quotedLanguage: you will want to ask your lender to waive the deficiency before you go through with a short sale. In some states, after a short sale, your lender could sue you to collect the amount of the deficiency. Getting a waiver of deficiency means that the lender waived the right to collect this amount. If the lender waives the deficiency, get the waiver in writing and keep it for your records.
claims.notes: ⚠️ The CFPB says 'in some states'. It does NOT say whether Idaho is one of them for a short sale, and no Idaho statute read for this guide addresses a deficiency after a short sale. Do not write 'Idaho lenders can sue after a short sale' or the reverse. State the CFPB's advice and send the reader to an Idaho attorney.

claims.claim: The CFPB defines a deed-in-lieu of foreclosure as an arrangement in which the owner voluntarily turns over ownership of the home to the lender to avoid the foreclosure process.
claims.quotedLanguage: A deed-in-lieu of foreclosure is an arrangement where you voluntarily turn over ownership of your home to the lender to avoid the foreclosure process.
claims.notes: Consumer-education definition. 'Arrangement' implies the lender takes part; the lender is the party that receives the deed. No source read says a lender must accept one. The effect of junior liens on a deed in lieu was NOT sourced; do not discuss it as fact.

claims.claim: The CFPB advises anyone considering a deed-in-lieu to make sure it covers the entire amount still owed on the mortgage loan, says the borrower can ask the lender to waive any deficiency and should get that waiver in writing, and warns that a tax liability may still arise.
claims.quotedLanguage: If you are considering a deed-in-lieu of foreclosure, make sure that it covers the entire amount of money you still owe on the mortgage loan. ... you can ask your lender to waive the deficiency. If the lender agrees, ask for the waiver in writing and keep it for your records. You may still incur a tax liability, so you may want to speak with a tax professional or attorney.
claims.notes: ⚠️ The CFPB page also says a deed-in-lieu 'may help you avoid being responsible for any amount left on the mortgage'. That is 'may', conditioned on the agreement. Never write that a deed in lieu wipes out the debt.

claims.claim: The CFPB suggests that a borrower considering a deed-in-lieu also ask the lender or servicer about help with relocation expenses through private programs sometimes called cash-for-keys.
claims.quotedLanguage: also ask your lender or servicer about help with your relocation expenses through private programs that are sometimes called
claims.notes: A suggestion to ASK, not a promise that money is available. The short-sale page makes a similar suggestion in different words. No amount is sourced; never state one. Quote stops before the typographic quotation marks around the term.

claims.claim: For FHA-insured loans, HUD describes a Pre-Foreclosure Sale, also known as a short sale, as a home disposition option under which the servicer may be able to accept less than the full amount owed by approving eligible borrowers when the current market value is not enough to pay the loan in full. HUD says such an option may be offered when the borrower cannot continue paying even with a home retention option.
claims.quotedLanguage: you may be offered a home disposition option. ... If your current market value is not enough to pay the loan in full, your servicer may be able to accept less than the full amount owed by approving eligible borrowers for a Pre-Foreclosure Sale, also known as a short sale. You may be eligible to receive relocation expenses if you meet certain conditions.
claims.notes: ⚠️ FHA-INSURED LOANS ONLY. Must be stated with 'for FHA-insured loans'. Never generalise to conventional, VA or USDA loans. Eligibility conditions are not listed on the page; do not invent them. The HUD page shows no revision date.

claims.claim: For FHA-insured loans, HUD describes a Deed-in-Lieu of Foreclosure as something a borrower may be eligible for if unable to complete a Pre-Foreclosure Sale by the end of its marketing period: voluntarily offering to deed the property to HUD in exchange for a release from all obligations under the mortgage.
claims.quotedLanguage: If you are unable to complete a PFS transaction at the expiration of the PFS marketing period, you may be eligible to voluntarily offer to deed ... the property to HUD in exchange for a release from all obligations under the Mortgage.
claims.notes: ⚠️ FHA-INSURED LOANS ONLY, and 'may be eligible'. The 'release from all obligations under the Mortgage' wording is HUD's description of the FHA option; it is not a rule for other loan types and says nothing about tax. The length of the PFS marketing period is NOT on this page; do not state one. The elided words are HUD's parenthetical gloss in typographic quotes.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 45-1512 allows a money judgment to be sought for the balance due on the obligation at any time within 3 months after a sale under a deed of trust, and requires the complaint to set out the entire secured indebtedness, the amount the property sold for and the fair market value at the date of sale.
claims.quotedLanguage: At any time within 3 months after any sale under a deed of trust, as hereinbefore provided, a money judgment may be sought for the balance due upon the obligation for which such deed of trust was given as security, and in such action the plaintiff shall set forth in his complaint the entire amount of indebtedness which was secured by such deed of trust and the amount for which the same was sold and the fair market value at the date of sale
claims.notes: ⚠️ This section applies after a SALE UNDER A DEED OF TRUST (a trustee's sale). It does not mention a short sale or a deed in lieu. Use it to show what a completed foreclosure can lead to, never as the rule for a short sale or deed in lieu. The statute writes '3 months' as a numeral. Whether a lender actually seeks such a judgment is a fact question; never predict it.

claims.claim: Under Idaho Code 45-1512 the court must find the fair market value of the property at the time of the trustee's sale, may not render judgment for more than the amount by which the indebtedness due at the time of sale exceeds that fair market value, with interest from the date of sale, and in no event for more than the difference between the sale price and the entire secured indebtedness.
claims.quotedLanguage: Before rendering judgment the court shall find the fair market value of the real property sold at the time of sale. The court may not render judgment for more than the amount by which the entire amount of indebtedness due at the time of sale exceeds the fair market value at that time, with interest from date of sale, but in no event may the judgment exceed the difference between the amount for which such property was sold and the entire amount of the indebtedness secured by the deed of trust.
claims.notes: Two limits, both must be stated: (1) indebtedness minus court-found fair market value, with interest; (2) never more than indebtedness minus sale price. Do not run an example with invented dollar figures. Applies after a trustee's sale only.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 6-101 provides that there can be but one action to recover a debt secured by a mortgage on real estate, that the court may direct a sale of the property, and that if the sheriff's return shows the proceeds are insufficient and a balance remains due, judgment can be docketed for that balance against the defendants personally liable for the debt, becoming a lien on the judgment debtor's real estate.
claims.quotedLanguage: There can be but one action for the recovery of any debt, or the enforcement of any right secured by mortgage upon real estate which action must be in accordance with the provisions of this chapter. ... (and if it appear from the sheriff's return that the proceeds are insufficient, and a balance still remains due, judgment can then be docketed for such balance against the defendant or defendants personally liable for the debt), and it becomes a lien on the real estate of such judgment debtor, as in other cases on which execution may be issued.
claims.notes: ⚠️ JUDICIAL MORTGAGE FORECLOSURE. Subsection (3) lists many proceedings that are NOT an 'action' for this purpose, including exercise of a trust-deed power of sale under 45-1505. Do not summarise the 'one action' rule as a blanket protection, and do not apply it to a reader. Must be paired with 6-108 (the cap). The section also says these sales are subject to redemption; that is outside this guide's scope.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 6-108 bars any Idaho court from entering a deficiency judgment in a mortgage foreclosure on real property for more than the difference between the mortgage indebtedness as determined by the decree, plus costs of foreclosure and sale, and the reasonable value of the mortgaged property as determined by the court on evidence.
claims.quotedLanguage: No court in the state of Idaho shall have jurisdiction to enter a deficiency judgment in any case involving a foreclosure of a mortgage on real property in any amount greater than the difference between the mortgage indebtedness, as determined by the decree, plus costs of foreclosure and sale, and the reasonable value of the mortgaged property, to be determined by the court in the decree upon the taking of evidence of such value.
claims.notes: Wording differs from 45-1512: 'reasonable value' here, 'fair market value' there. Keep each term with its own section. Applies to 'a foreclosure of a mortgage on real property'; it does not mention a short sale or deed in lieu.

claims.claim: The IRS states that, in general, when a debt is canceled, forgiven or discharged for less than the amount owed, the canceled amount is taxable and must be reported on the return for the year the cancellation occurred, and that for an owner of property securing a debt, cancellation may occur through foreclosure, repossession, voluntary transfer of the property to the lender, abandonment, or a mortgage modification.
claims.quotedLanguage: If you own property securing a debt, cancellation of the debt may occur due to foreclosure, repossession, voluntary transfer of the property to the lender, abandonment of the property, or a mortgage modification. ... In general, if your debt is canceled, forgiven, or discharged for less than the amount owed, the amount of the canceled debt is taxable. If taxable, you must report the canceled debt on your tax return for the year in which the cancellation occurred.
claims.notes: ⚠️ 'In general'. The same page lists exceptions and exclusions; always state this rule together with the fact that exclusions exist (see ss-irs-bankruptcy-insolvency-exclusions) and with the tax-professional pointer. FEDERAL only. Idaho state income tax treatment of canceled debt was NOT sourced. Topic 431 page reads 'Page Last Reviewed or Updated: 24-Sep-2026'.

claims.claim: As published by the IRS and read on 2026-11-13, the exclusion from income for canceled qualified principal residence indebtedness covers debt discharged before January 1, 2026, or discharged subject to an arrangement entered into and evidenced in writing before January 1, 2026. IRS Publication 4681 (2025) states that this indebtedness cannot be excluded from income for discharges completed or discharge agreements entered into after December 31, 2025, and the Instructions for Forms 1099-A and 1099-C state that the exclusion expires on December 31, 2025.
claims.quotedLanguage: Cancellation of qualified principal residence indebtedness that is discharged before January 1, 2026, or discharged subject to an arrangement that is entered into and evidenced in writing before January 1, 2026 ... Qualified principal residence indebtedness cannot be excluded from income for discharges completed or discharge agreements entered into after December 31, 2025. ... The exclusion from income of discharged mortgage debt for qualified principal residence indebtedness and qualified student loan debt under section 108(f)(5) expires on December 31, 2025.
claims.notes: 🚨 HIGHEST-RISK CLAIM ON THE PAGE. Three IRS pages agree as of 2026-11-13 (Topic 431 last reviewed 24-Sep-2026; Pub 4681 is the 2025 edition 'For use in preparing 2025 Returns'; Form 1099-A/C instructions 'Revised: 04/2025'). No 2026-edition Pub 4681 existed at access. Congress can change this, including retroactively, and Pub 4681 itself points to IRS.gov/Pub4681 for 'legislation enacted after it was published'. ALWAYS state with the access date, attributed to the IRS, with the written-arrangement-before-2026 carve-out, and with the tax-professional pointer. NEVER write 'forgiven mortgage debt is taxable in 2026' as a flat rule: other exclusions (insolvency, bankruptcy) are still listed, and the recourse/nonrecourse distinction matters. RE-CHECK all three pages before every republication and in January 2027 when the 2026 forms publish. MEDIUM because of volatility, not because the quotes are unclear.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 431 lists, among the exclusions of canceled debt from gross income, debt canceled in a Title 11 bankruptcy case and debt canceled to the extent the taxpayer was insolvent. Publication 4681 explains that a taxpayer was insolvent immediately before the cancellation to the extent total liabilities exceeded the fair market value of all assets at that time. Topic 431 says an amount qualifying for exclusion is reported on Form 982, attached to the return.
claims.quotedLanguage: Debt canceled in a Title 11 bankruptcy case ... Debt canceled to the extent insolvent ... You were insolvent immediately before the cancellation to the extent that the total of all of your liabilities was more than the FMV of all of your assets immediately before the cancellation. ... You must report the amount qualifying for exclusion, and any corresponding reduction of those tax attributes on Form 982, Reduction of Tax Attributes Due to Discharge of Indebtedness (and Section 1082 Basis Adjustment) and attach to your tax return.
claims.notes: ⚠️ Never tell a reader they are insolvent or that an exclusion applies to them. Pub 4681 counts ALL assets, including exempt ones such as retirement accounts, so the test is not intuitive. Excluding debt generally requires reducing tax attributes. Describe, attribute, refer to a tax professional. The insolvency definition is from the 2025 edition of Pub 4681.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 431 cautions that when a creditor takes property securing a debt in full or partial satisfaction of it, the owner is treated as having sold the property to the creditor, and the tax treatment depends on whether the owner was personally liable (recourse debt) or not (nonrecourse debt). For recourse debt, ordinary income from cancellation is the amount by which the discharged debt exceeds the property's fair market value; for nonrecourse debt there is no ordinary income from debt cancellation.
claims.quotedLanguage: If your debt is secured by property, and the creditor takes that property in full or partial satisfaction of your debt, you are treated as having sold that property to the creditor. The tax treatment of the deemed sale depends on whether you were personally liable for the debt (recourse debt) or not personally liable for the debt (nonrecourse debt). ... Your ordinary income from the cancellation of the debt is the amount by which the discharged debt exceeds the FMV of the property. ... You will not have ordinary income resulting from debt cancellation.
claims.notes: ⚠️ Do NOT tell a reader whether an Idaho home loan is recourse or nonrecourse for federal tax purposes; no source read answers that, and it turns on the loan and state law. The deemed sale can also produce a gain or loss separate from canceled-debt income; Topic 431 sends readers to Pub 4681, Pub 544 and Pub 523 for that. Keep it descriptive.

claims.claim: IRS instructions direct a covered creditor to file Form 1099-C for each debtor for whom it canceled a debt of $600 or more when an identifiable event has occurred, and list among identifiable events a discharge under an agreement between creditor and debtor to cancel the debt at less than full consideration, giving short sales as the example. Topic 431 adds that the taxpayer's responsibility to report the correct taxable amount remains regardless of the accuracy of the Form 1099-C received.
claims.quotedLanguage: File Form 1099-C, Cancellation of Debt, for each debtor for whom you canceled a debt owed to you of $600 or more if: ... A discharge of indebtedness under an agreement between the creditor and the debtor to cancel the debt at less than full consideration (for example, short sales). ... Your responsibility to report the correct taxable amount of canceled debt as income on your tax return for the year in which the cancellation occurred remains, regardless of the accuracy of the Form 1099-C you received.
claims.notes: The $600 figure is the CREDITOR's filing threshold, not a threshold below which canceled debt is tax-free. Only entities described under 'Who Must File' are covered; do not write 'every lender'. A Form 1099-C is an information return, not a tax bill. Instructions read 'Revised: 04/2025'.

claims.claim: The CFPB describes a housing counselor through a HUD-approved agency as specially trained and certified by the government to help a borrower assess their financial situation, evaluate options when having trouble paying a mortgage, and make a plan. It states that HUD-approved housing counseling agencies provide foreclosure prevention counseling free of charge and can help a borrower talk to the mortgage servicer and understand the options offered.
claims.quotedLanguage: A housing counselor though a HUD-approved agency is specially trained and certified by the government to help you assess your financial situation, evaluate options if you are having trouble paying your mortgage loan, and make a plan to get you help with your mortgage. ... HUD-approved housing counseling agencies provide foreclosure prevention counseling free of charge. They can also help you talk to your mortgage servicer and understand any options your servicer has offered.
claims.notes: 'though' is the CFPB's own typo for 'through'; it is kept verbatim in the quote and must not be reproduced in prose. The same page says a counselor cannot promise the borrower will keep the home, and that someone facing imminent foreclosure or served with legal papers may also need an attorney. The avoid-foreclosure guide in this cluster may claim the same page under its own prefix; dedupe at merge.
